text.p: U.S. Borax Inc, the world's largest borate producer, said on Monday it would spend up to US$5 million to identify new markets.

Faced with declining usage in detergents in the U.S. and poor year-end sales to the agricultral fertilisers sector, Borax hopes to expand borate consumption to other sectors, Borax chairman and chief executive Ian White-Thomson told Reuters.
"It will be more than US$1 million, but probably no more than US$5 million," White-Thomson said.
The key use for borate is making glass fibre insulation.
Borax is owned by RTZ-CRA.
The state of the industry is largely a reflection of the construction market and the economy, White-Thomson said.
Borate can be found in items ranging from insecticide to anti-freeze to the company's best known product "20 Mule Team Borax" a detergent bleaching agent.

A growing tension among U.S. consumers for washing clothes in cold water, not requiring bleach, has helped refocus some of Borax's marketing efforts on Europe and developing countries of Asia and Latin America where hot water washing is more prominent, White-Thomson said.
Sales at Borax, which average about US$500 million a year, have been hindered by an over-supply of ceramic goods, which typically contain borates, White-Thomson said.

In the last few years, the large ceramic manufacturing centres, mainly based in the Mediterranean, have been running at full capacity, creating a huge inventory base that only now is being worked down, White-Thomson said.
China also has been a lacklustre market for Borax, as efforts to establish a stronger presence there have been countered by a rise in domestic output.
"We had made quite good penetration into China last year ... what happened is local production has increased so we haven't made the gains we'd hoped for," he said.
Borax's main competitor, Turkey's state-run Etibank, also is looking to expand its markets internationally, he said.

Etibank's share of the world borate market has climbed to about 31 percent in recent years, growth which has come at the expense of Borax, which has seen its command of the marketplace dip to around 48 percent, White-Thomson said.

A key user of borates, Procter and Gamble Co, in its Tide With Bleach brand laundry detergent, holds a patent on the formula for activating the bleaching process, which other detergent makers do not hold.
As a result, borate requirements among the other detergent makers, are less. "It's closely patented and none of the others can access that," White-Thomson said.
White-Thomson said he expected a small dip in the U.S. housing market this year, which would affect demand for borates used in insulation, tiling and other building sectors.

"As a result, we'll see a small dip in demand, probably," he said. However, this could be countered by a resurgence in demand from the agricultural and other specialty markets for borates, White-Thomson said. For its part, Borax is making gains in productivity while reducing its payroll, he said.
Man-hours of borate-produced has risen to 0.43 tonnes per person in 1995 from 0.35 tonnes in 1992.
Exploration is also underway to find new borate deposits to replace the Boron, California, mine set to expire in about 40 years.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
